subject: Accounting
title: Arthur Andersen's Downfall
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Arthur Andersen's Downfall.

hook.text: Arthur Andersen was one of the Big Five accounting firms. Enron destroyed it.

buildup.text: Andersen audited Enron for years and gave clean opinions on fraudulent financial statements.

discovery.text: When the scandal broke, Andersen employees shredded thousands of documents overnight.

twist.text: The Supreme Court later overturned Andersen's conviction—but it was too late. Clients had fled.

climax.text: A 90-year-old firm with 85,000 employees ceased to exist. The Big Five became the Big Four.

quiz.question: Why did Arthur Andersen collapse?
options: It shredded documents and lost client trust after Enron
It was bought by a competitor

details.summary: Arthur Andersen, once one of the Big Five accounting firms, collapsed after its role in the Enron scandal. This topic covers how conflict of interest between auditing and consulting services led to compromised audits and the firm's destruction.
details.whyItMatters: The death of Arthur Andersen proved that even the most prestigious firms can be destroyed by ethical failures. It permanently changed the relationship between auditors and their clients.
takeaways: Arthur Andersen earned more from consulting fees at Enron than from audit fees, creating a massive conflict
The firm was convicted of obstruction of justice for shredding Enron-related documents
Its collapse reduced the Big Five to the Big Four and reshaped the entire audit industry

faq.question: Why did Arthur Andersen collapse?
faq.answer: Arthur Andersen was Enron's auditor and was convicted of obstruction of justice for shredding documents related to the Enron fraud. The conviction destroyed client confidence, and the firm surrendered its licenses in 2002, going from 85,000 employees to zero.

faq.question: How did Arthur Andersen's downfall change the audit industry?
faq.answer: It reduced the Big Five to Big Four, eliminated the practice of firms providing both audit and lucrative consulting to the same client, and directly inspired the Sarbanes-Oxley Act's requirements for auditor independence and the creation of the PCAOB.
